title: Playing around New Orleans before Chicago and the 'Slap Tongue King'
summary: He was only starting in the New Orleans scene when he left for Oliver; he worked with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Manuel Perez and Piron, learned from Amos White, and was known as the Slap Tongue King until broken reeds cost too much.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Were you a part of the music scene at all in New Orleans or did you become a part of the music scene when you got to Chicago?

I was just beginning to be a part of the music scene in New Orleans, but then when I got the opportunity to go to Chicago, then I went to Chicago. I went to join King Oliver. I had heard so much about him and I wanted to go and so I left then. But I was getting to be a part of the scene in New Orleans.
What musicians did you work with?

I worked with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly. I worked with Manuel Perez. I had an opportunity to work with him. And I worked with Piron. Another fantastic trumpet man that nobody don't hear anything about is Amos White, and he's a professor at Berklee College of Music -- in music, a very fantastic man. He taught me a lot. And we had a band together and he took me around, and all these supposed to be big-time clarinetists like Picou, he showed me where they wasn't nothing. He did, too. Because he liked me and he was very interested in me, like my second father. He took good care of me. He taught me a lot of music, too.
I had a wonderful time, but I left. I was known as the "Slap Tongue King."
Yes. Oh, I was good, but I started breaking too many reeds and it cost me, because it was too much money, I said, "I have to cut that out." And I left, and that's history.
